implementation_notes: TypeScript contributes no runtime of its own here: Promise, thenables and async/await are the JavaScript semantics the compiler targets, typed as Promise<T> with async functions returning Promise<T> and helpers such as Awaited<T> and the tuple inference of Promise.all. The compiler either keeps async/await native (--target ES2017 and later) or downlevels it into generator-based helpers for older targets. The classic structure is therefore absent from application code - a typed pending value is stored and awaited as Promise<T> - and an explicit deferred promise is written only to wrap a callback API.
pitfalls: TypeScript does not flag a dropped promise: an unawaited Promise<T> is a perfectly well-typed expression, so only a linter rule (no-floating-promises) points out the handle whose rejection will escape.
An async function never throws synchronously - a failure becomes a rejected promise - so a try/catch around the call site instead of around an await silently misses it.

Downleveling async/await below ES2017 emits generator-based helpers and depends on a Promise implementation being present at runtime; check the configured target and lib before assuming native behaviour.
